Stump Grinding From Our Home Yard Since 1982

Auburn Township is Roubic's home base — the yard on Taylor May Rd has been the family's operating hub since 1982. Most Auburn Township grinding starts as a follow-up to a Roubic removal, but we also grind stumps other contractors left behind, storm-fallen trees homeowners cleared themselves, and stumps inherited with a property purchase.

Auburn Township Local Knowledge

The 811 Utility Mark-Out Before Any Grind

Underground utility mark-out through the Ohio Utilities Protection Service (OUPS / 811) is required before grinding any stump — the grinder wheel reaches well below grade, and gas, water, and buried electric lines are common on Auburn Township's rural-suburban lots. Roubic schedules the OUPS locate at booking, so lines are flagged before the crew arrives. There is no homeowner filing step.

On larger 1–10+ acre parcels, we walk the grind path with you at the estimate to confirm septic fields, sprinkler lines, and invisible-fence runs that OUPS does not cover.

Scheduled by Roubic before every grind — no homeowner action needed

What Happens If You Defer

The Cost of Leaving the Stump — Auburn Township Context

Three reasons a leftover stump gets more expensive the longer it sits.

Regrowth & Suckering

Live maple and other stumps push suckers and root sprouts, and hardy species can re-establish. Grinding out the crown stops regrowth for good instead of fighting it every season.

Pest & Decay Harborage

A decaying stump becomes a nest for carpenter ants, termites, and wood-boring beetles — close to the house on wooded Auburn Township lots, that's a pest problem you pay for later.

Trip Hazard & Mowing Obstruction

A hidden stump in the lawn is a mower-blade killer and a liability trip hazard. Grinding it below grade recovers usable yard and clears the way for sod, pavers, or a replant.

Common Auburn Township Grinding Questions

Auburn Township Stump Grinding FAQ

Six things Auburn Township homeowners want to know before booking.

How much does stump grinding cost in Auburn Township?
Grinding starts at a $275 minimum per visit. Most single residential stumps (12–30" DBH) run $200–$400. Heritage 60"+ stumps that need the full-size track grinder run $400–$800. Multiple stumps at the same address earn a per-stump discount, and grinding paired with a Roubic removal qualifies for a same-job package rate ($50–$150 less than booking it separately). Every estimate is free and quoted on-site.
Will Roubic grind a stump from a tree another company removed?
Yes. We routinely grind stumps from removals other contractors handled, storm-fallen trees the homeowner cleared, and stumps inherited with a property purchase. Booking is the same as any other grinding job and the standard $275 minimum applies.
How deep does Roubic grind stumps in Auburn Township?
Our standard grind takes the stump 6–12 inches below grade — deep enough to plant grass, lay sod, install pavers, or pour a small concrete pad over. We can grind deeper on request if you're planning new construction or replanting a tree in the same spot.
Do you clean up the chips after grinding?
Yes — full chip cleanup is the default. Optional topsoil backfill is available for an additional fee if you want the hole filled and ready for grass seed. If you'd rather keep the grindings as mulch elsewhere on your property, we'll leave them at no charge.
Do I need a utility mark-out before grinding?
Yes — an Ohio Utilities Protection Service (OUPS / 811) mark-out is required before grinding because the wheel reaches below grade near buried gas, water, and electric lines. Roubic schedules the 811 locate at booking, so lines are flagged before the crew arrives. There's no homeowner filing step. On larger lots we also confirm septic, sprinkler, and invisible-fence runs at the estimate.
Is Roubic licensed and insured for stump grinding?
Yes — Roubic Tree & Landscape LLC carries full general liability and workers-compensation insurance, with continuous coverage since 1982. Certificates of insurance are provided on request before any work begins, which is common for HOA and property-manager grinding jobs.
